title: Music Composition and Audio Engineering
answer: Score generation, stem separation, drum programming, mixing and mastering, and generated foley.

children.name: Score Generation and Composition
children.blurb: Score generation and composition covers systems that produce musical notation, MIDI data, or full audio arrangements from a prompt, a melody, a chord progression, or a style description.

children.name: Stem Separation and Restoration
children.blurb: Stem separation and restoration covers the work of pulling a finished recording apart into its component parts, typically vocals, drums, bass and a residual instrumental, and of repairing damage in old or badly captured audio.

children.name: Generative Rhythm and Drum Programming
children.blurb: Generative rhythm and drum programming covers the use of AI systems to create, vary, or complete drum patterns and rhythmic parts for music production.

children.name: Automated Mixing and Mastering
children.blurb: Automated mixing and mastering covers software that balances levels, shapes tone, controls dynamics and prepares a finished track for release with limited or no human intervention.

children.name: Generated Foley and Sound Design
children.blurb: Generated Foley and Sound Design covers the use of AI models to create everyday sound effects, ambiences and layered audio beds for film, television, games and podcasts.

sections.body: Artificial intelligence in music composition and audio engineering covers systems that write or extend musical material, take finished recordings apart into their component instruments, program rhythms, shape a mix, and create sound effects that were never recorded. In practice this means a composer can prompt a model for a string arrangement and edit the result, a producer can pull a vocal out of a stereo master that was never multitracked, and a game studio can generate footsteps or wind without booking a foley stage. The work is mostly assistive rather than autonomous. Models are good at producing plausible material in a known style and at the signal processing tasks of separation and level balancing, and they are weak at long form structure, intent, and the kind of decision that comes from knowing what a piece is for. The tools sit inside existing digital audio workstations rather than replacing them, and the human still chooses, edits, and commits.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Stem separation is the most settled area. Source separation models now isolate vocals, drums, bass and other instruments from mixed recordings well enough for remix, sampling and restoration work, though artifacts remain audible on dense or heavily compressed material and on anything with unusual instrumentation. Score generation produces usable sketches, accompaniments and variations, but coherence over several minutes and sensitivity to a brief are unreliable, and notation output often needs cleanup. Drum programming and rhythm generation are strong at style imitation and variation, weaker at groove that responds to a specific performance. Automated mixing and mastering can match loudness targets and apply learned tonal balance, yet it does not hear the song the way a mixing engineer does, and it struggles with material that falls outside its training distribution. Generated foley and sound design are convincing for short, textural sounds and less so for anything requiring physical specificity. Rights, consent and credit around training data and generated output remain unresolved, and no system here understands music in the way a trained musician does.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages run roughly from writing music to shaping and finishing it. Score Generation and Composition is the entry point for material itself, covering how models propose melodies, harmony and arrangement and where those proposals break down. Generative Rhythm and Drum Programming narrows to the timekeeping layer, where pattern generation, variation and groove are handled. Stem Separation and Restoration sits apart as the analysis side, dealing with pulling apart and repairing existing recordings, and it is the page to read if the question is what can be recovered from a finished mix. Automated Mixing and Mastering covers the processing chain that balances and finalizes a track, including what loudness matching and learned tonal decisions can and cannot do. Generated Foley and Sound Design closes the set by moving from music to non musical audio, covering synthesized effects and ambience for film, games and other media. Read together they describe a pipeline, and read separately each answers a different practical question about where a model helps and where a person still has to decide.
